name: example-nextjs
description: Example profile for a Next.js App Router site behind a CDN, an HAProxy edge and a caching reverse proxy. Copy it, put YOUR measured numbers in, and keep it in your own private repo — a profile contains hostnames and URL pools, i.e. information about your infrastructure.

public._comment: through the CDN. ⚠️ measures the CDN, not your origin — and costs you egress.

edge._comment: your own edge load balancer, CDN bypassed, SNI and Host still correct. Put the edge address in bypass. This is normally the target you want.

proxy-node._comment: a single caching-proxy node: isolates one node and skips the load balancer.

app-instance._comment: one application instance directly, to get per-instance capacity. Routes served only by the reverse proxy answer 404 here, so skip those classes or one class goes to 100% failed and trips the brake at a few req/s.

auth._comment: Authenticated classes. Sign-in is the component that anonymous profiles cannot reach, and on a real campaign it was the only one that saturated: the web tier held over 7,000 concurrent users while login topped out at ~150/s. Password grant ('Direct Access Grants' in Keycloak) is what a load test can drive; if your client only allows Authorization Code + PKCE, use a dedicated test client instead of scripting the form.
auth._client_secret_comment: Only for confidential clients. Prefer a public client for load tests: a secret in a profile is a secret in a file that gets copied around.
auth._users_comment: Credentials come from a CSV (`username,password` per line). Pass the path as CROWDSIM_AUTH_USERS at run time and leave it OUT of the profile: profiles get shared, secrets should not travel with them. One account per virtual user, so the run stays reproducible and you do not measure one user's sessions.
auth._logout_comment: Sessions are a resource: 150 logins/s for one minute is 9,000 sessions on the identity provider, and the memory they hold changes the result of the NEXT run. Turn this on (with logout_url) when you need two runs to be comparable; it costs one extra request per iteration.

_classes_comment: The MIX. Weights are the share of user requests/s you measured on your own edge access log during the spike you want to replay — not a guess, and not a uniform split. Only count requests the client makes: server-side sub-requests the app issues by itself are a CONSEQUENCE, and generating them yourself would double-count. `--peak` is the total; each class gets weight/total × peak.
_log_match_comment: `log_match` is how `crowdsim weights` recognises a class in that access log: a list of path globs, anchored at the start of the path, where `*` spans slashes. It has NO effect on a run — a profile without it generates identical traffic, it just cannot have its mix measured. Without a rule a class is matched by its `path_prefix` and by membership of its own pool, plus the hard filter that an `rsc` class only ever matches a request carrying the navigation parameter. Nothing is inferred from a URL's shape: whatever no class claims is reported as an unclassified share, which is the number that tells you the mix is incomplete.

classes.name: rsc_page
classes.label: RSC navigation
classes._comment: React Server Components prefetch and navigation. Usually the largest class and the one flat load tools cannot produce.
classes._slo_comment: max_p95_ms here is THIS class's own limit, sharper than the profile's 5000 ms: a navigation request at 2.5 s means the app is already queueing, and waiting for the shared limit spends a minute measuring a system that was already gone. A per-class limit may only be SHARPER than the profile's — looser is refused by validate, since it would move the knee later than the profile asks for. max_failed_rate works the same way.

classes.name: html
classes.label: HTML document
classes._comment: landings and reloads: full server-rendered documents.

classes.name: rsc_search
classes.label: RSC search
classes._comment: search is frequently the most expensive class per request. Keep it separate: averaging it into the others hides the thing that actually falls over.

classes.name: static
classes.label: static asset
classes._comment: assets that are served BY THE APP rather than by the CDN. Regenerate this pool after every deploy: it contains build hashes. The pool below is empty, so this class is dropped from a run — but log_match still lets `crowdsim weights` count these requests instead of reporting them as unclassified.

classes._rate_comment: A class may declare `"rate_rps": 150` INSTEAD of a weight, when the question is about that class alone — "the login saturates at ~150 login/s" is a finding about one class, and solving for it through a weight is arithmetic in the wrong direction. The pinned classes get exactly what they ask for and the rest split WHAT IS LEFT by weight, so `--peak` keeps meaning the total — which is what the safe-peak gate reads, so a per-class rate is not a way past a ceiling. A profile whose fixed rates already exceed `--peak` is refused, naming both numbers: they are never scaled down to fit.
classes.name: proxy_only
classes.label: proxy-only route
classes._comment: a route the reverse proxy serves and the app instance does not. Listed to show path_prefix; skipped on the app-instance target.

classes.name: login
classes.label: sign-in
classes._comment: Not cacheable by definition: every login reaches the identity provider, which burns CPU verifying the password on purpose. This is usually the first class to knee.

classes.name: authed_api
classes.label: API, signed in
classes._comment: Reads with a bearer token. Needs a `login` class in the same profile: the token comes from there, and it is refreshed automatically when it expires mid-ramp or the API answers 401 — otherwise this class would collapse to 100% failures and trip the brake for a reason that is not the system's.

classes.name: signup
classes.label: registration
classes._comment: Every iteration registers a NEW identity: replaying one address would create the account on the first request and measure the conflict on every one after. The accounts it creates are real — plan the cleanup before you run it.

pools._comment: Pools can be inlined like above, or pulled from a sibling file with "@pool-pages.json" — which is what `crowdsim discover` writes. Keep pools OUT of a public repo: they are a map of your site.

rsc.mode_comment: In a real Next.js build the _rsc value depends on route+build, not on the request: one measured event had tens of thousands of RSC requests collapsing onto ~13 distinct values. That repetitiveness is the entire premise of 'a shared micro-cache would absorb most of this'. RSC_MODE=repeat replays it; RSC_MODE=random tests the opposite hypothesis.

_cache_headers_comment: Which response header tells you the cache state of each layer, and what counts as a hit. crowdsim reports a hit ratio per layer per class from these, and `probe` states a verdict per layer for one request. Three answers, not two: hit, miss, and NEVER APPEARED — the last one means this profile names a header the layer does not send, which looks exactly like a cold cache and is not. It is reported as unknown, never as a miss.

slo._comment: guillotine_ms is your reverse proxy read timeout: requests slower than this become 504s for real users, so crowdsim reports the share that crossed it. brake_class is the class whose p95 aborts the run — for the classes that declare no limit of their own. Whatever is crossed first stops the run, and the summary's aborted_by names which class and which threshold it was.

safety._comment: allow_hosts is a hard gate: crowdsim refuses any target whose host does not match. safe_peak_rps is the ceiling above which --i-know-this-breaks-production is mandatory. Set safe_peak_rps to a level you have already proven harmless, not to what you hope is harmless. Neither field has a default anywhere, and allow_hosts declared as [] is an error rather than an empty allowlist — `crowdsim init` leaves both blank on purpose, and validate refuses the file until a human fills them in.
safety._generator_mbps_comment: Optional: what the GENERATOR's link can actually sustain, in Mbit/s. `probe` measures the weight of one page, so `load` and `doctor` can tell you what the requested peak implies (45 KB at 380 req/s is ~17.6 MB/s = ~141 Mbit/s) and warn before a run comes back with generator_ok: false. It is a warning, never a gate: the estimate assumes every request weighs what that page weighed, which is wrong in both directions.

discover._comment: strip_prefix_regex removes locale prefixes that the site redirects: testing a 307 measures the redirect, not the render.

journey._think_time_comment: The reading pauses between pages. Half of any concurrency figure: concurrency is sessions/s × session duration, and the session duration IS the fan-out plus these pauses. Two shapes — { "min_ms": 2000, "max_ms": 9000 } for a declared range, or { "samples": [820, 1400, 3100], "measured": true } for pauses somebody actually observed, which is what `crowdsim record` writes from a browser recording. Declare nothing and the generator uses 1000-5000 ms, the value it has always used — and the run says `default`, so a concurrency figure is never read as if the pace had been measured.
journey._comment: Only needed for --shape journey: a recorded fan-out of {path, rsc[], static[]} per page. Record it with a real browser against your own site.
